title: Python Foundations: From Execution to a Tested Progress Tracker
description: A beginner course that teaches Python through explicit runtime models, worked code, boundary tests, guided practice, and a capstone progress tracker. Learners predict behavior, run evidence-producing programs, explain failures, and revise code rather than memorizing syntax alone.
prerequisites: Ability to create and save a text file
learningOutcomes: Explain how Python evaluates statements, binds names, and reports errors
Use types, conditions, loops, functions, and collections in small tested programs
Build and explain a modular progress tracker with validation and boundary tests

modules.summary: Build a correct mental model of Python execution, values, types, conversion, and observable output.
objectives: Write and explain small Python programs

lessons.title: Running Python and Working with Values
lessons.summary: Python executes source from top to bottom while names refer to objects. This lesson establishes the edit-run-observe cycle, assignment, naming rules, and how to inspect values without treating a variable as a fixed box.
objectives: Explain and apply the Python behavior taught in Running Python and Working with Values
Test the behavior with a small observable program

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: Python programs are sequences of statements evaluated by the interpreter. An assignment such as `price = 120` evaluates the expression on the right and binds the resulting integer object to the name on the left. Reassignment changes the binding; it does not alter the earlier object. Use descriptive snake_case names, keep one purpose per name, and inspect uncertain values with `print()` and `type()`. A `NameError` means a name was used before a successful binding. Reading the traceback from its final line upward usually identifies both the exception and the line that caused it.

blocks.heading: Worked Python example
blocks.bodyMarkdown: Run this example, predict the output first, and then change one value at a time to observe cause and effect.
blocks.codeSource:
price = 120
quantity = 3
total = price * quantity
print(total)
print(type(total).__name__)

lessons.title: Types, Conversion, and Input/Output
lessons.summary: Values have types that determine supported operations. This lesson teaches strings, integers, floats, booleans, explicit conversion, formatted output, and safe handling of console input.
objectives: Explain and apply the Python behavior taught in Types, Conversion, and Input/Output
Test the behavior with a small observable program

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: `input()` always returns text, even when the user enters digits. Convert only after deciding the expected domain: `int()` for whole numbers and `float()` for decimal measurements. Conversion can raise `ValueError`, so user-facing programs should validate or handle failure rather than silently inventing a value. F-strings place evaluated expressions inside braces and preserve readable output logic. Equality compares values, while `is` checks object identity and should normally be reserved for singletons such as `None`. Python does not automatically combine strings and numbers with `+`; explicit conversion keeps intent visible.

lessons.title: Decisions with Conditions and Boolean Logic
lessons.summary: Conditional statements select behavior from explicit evidence. This lesson covers comparisons, truth values, if/elif/else, compound conditions, membership checks, and boundary testing.
objectives: Explain and apply the Python behavior taught in Decisions with Conditions and Boolean Logic
Test the behavior with a small observable program

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: An `if` statement executes its indented suite only when its condition is truthy. Use `elif` for mutually exclusive alternatives and `else` for the remaining case. Comparison chains such as `0 <= score <= 100` are clearer than repeating the variable. `and` requires both operands to be truthy, `or` requires at least one, and `not` reverses truth. Boundary values deserve explicit tests: a rule written as `score > 60` excludes 60, while `score >= 60` includes it. Avoid deeply nested conditions by naming meaningful booleans or returning early from functions.

blocks.heading: Worked Python example
blocks.bodyMarkdown: Run this example, predict the output first, and then change one value at a time to observe cause and effect.
blocks.codeSource:
score = 72
submitted = True
if 0 <= score <= 100 and submitted:
    result = "recorded"
else:
    result = "review input"
print(result)

lessons.title: Iteration with for, while, and range
lessons.summary: Loops repeat a well-defined operation. This lesson teaches iteration over collections, numeric ranges, accumulator patterns, controlled while loops, break, continue, and prevention of infinite loops.
objectives: Explain and apply the Python behavior taught in Iteration with for, while, and range
Test the behavior with a small observable program

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: A `for` loop asks an iterable for values one at a time; it is preferred when traversing a known collection. `range(start, stop, step)` excludes `stop`, a common source of off-by-one defects. An accumulator starts with an identity value—zero for addition, one for multiplication, or an empty collection for gathering—and updates once per iteration. A `while` loop is appropriate when repetition depends on changing state; its body must make progress toward termination. Use `break` for a deliberate early exit and `continue` to skip only the current iteration, but avoid them when a clearer loop condition expresses the rule.

blocks.heading: Worked Python example
blocks.bodyMarkdown: Run this example, predict the output first, and then change one value at a time to observe cause and effect.
blocks.codeSource:
scores = [70, 82, 91]
total = 0
for score in scores:
    total += score
average = total / len(scores)
print(average)

lessons.title: Functions, Parameters, and Return Values
lessons.summary: Functions package behavior behind a clear contract. This lesson covers definition, calls, parameters, return values, local scope, default arguments, documentation, and simple tests.
objectives: Explain and apply the Python behavior taught in Functions, Parameters, and Return Values
Test the behavior with a small observable program

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: A function should perform one coherent task and communicate through parameters and a return value. `return` ends the current call and provides a value to the caller; `print` only displays text and therefore is not a substitute for a return value. Parameters are local names bound when the function is called. Avoid depending on mutable global state because it hides inputs and complicates testing. Default values belong after required parameters and should be immutable in beginner code; use `None` when a fresh list or dictionary is needed for each call. A concise docstring states purpose, accepted inputs, returned output, and important failure behavior.

lessons.title: Collections and a Small Progress Tracker
lessons.summary: Lists, tuples, dictionaries, and sets model different relationships. This lesson applies their trade-offs in a small progress-tracker project and introduces safe decomposition.
objectives: Explain and apply the Python behavior taught in Collections and a Small Progress Tracker
Test the behavior with a small observable program

blocks.heading: Core model
blocks.bodyMarkdown: Choose a collection according to the operations the program needs. Lists preserve order and allow repeated values; tuples represent fixed-position records; dictionaries map unique keys to values; sets keep unique hashable members and provide efficient membership tests. Iterating over a dictionary yields keys, while `.items()` yields key-value pairs. Access with `mapping[key]` raises `KeyError` when absent; `.get(key, default)` expresses an expected fallback. Do not modify a list or dictionary structurally while iterating over the same view—build a new result or iterate over a copy. A useful small program separates input, domain calculation, and output formatting so each part can be tested.

finalAssessment.title: Learning Progress Tracker Capstone
finalAssessment.instructionsMarkdown: Build a command-line Python learning progress tracker. The program must add and update topics, validate percentages, list completed topics, calculate an average, handle invalid input without hiding unexpected defects, and separate domain logic from input/output. Include a README explaining design choices and at least ten assertions covering normal, boundary, and failure behavior.
deliverables: README with execution and design explanation
Recorded test output with at least ten assertions
Short reflection identifying one defect found through testing
